meta.title: Insecticide at night
authors: ER SIM clinical content team (draft prepared with Claude)
meta.guidelineBasis: Eddleston et al. early management protocol for OP/carbamate self-poisoning (Crit Care 2004); Eddleston & Chowdhury, Br J Clin Pharmacol 2016
meta.sourceNotes: Original ER SIM scenario. Not derived from any textbook case. Atropine titration, infusion and toxicity rules follow the Eddleston protocol. Pralidoxime left optional because evidence of benefit is uncertain. Doses and timings must be confirmed by the reviewing emergency physician before status APPROVED.
learningObjectives: Recognise the cholinergic toxidrome and start atropine within 5 minutes
Titrate atropine by doubling doses to clear chest, HR above 80 and SBP above 80
Start an infusion at 10–20% of the loading dose per hour once atropinised
Recognise recurrent cholinergic signs and atropine toxicity, and respond correctly
Secure the airway in respiratory failure, avoiding succinylcholine
Decontaminate with staff protection; avoid routine gastric lavage
Arrange ICU care, medico-legal registration and psychiatric assessment

patient.name: Rajan M.
patient.setting: District hospital emergency department, Kerala. ICU on site.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Drowsy, frothing and breathless after drinking insecticide 1 hour ago
presentation.triageNote: Paddy farmer brought by his wife and a neighbour by autorickshaw. Vomited twice on the way. Strong chemical smell. Triage: RED.

baselineExam.GENERAL: Drowsy but rousable. Drooling and sweating heavily. Vomit on his clothes with a strong kerosene-like smell.
baselineExam.HEENT: Pinpoint pupils (1 mm). Excess saliva and tears.
baselineExam.PULM: Coarse crackles and wheeze in both lungs (bronchorrhoea). Using accessory muscles.
baselineExam.CARD: Slow regular pulse about 48. Normal heart sounds.
baselineExam.ABD: Soft. Very active bowel sounds. Has passed loose stool.
baselineExam.SKIN: Cold, sweaty skin. Twitching (fasciculations) over the chest and thighs.
baselineExam.NEURO: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Generally weak; neck flexion 4/5. Reflexes present.

states.label: Cholinergic crisis
states.appearance: Drowsy, frothing at the mouth, sweating, breathing noisily.
states.patientSays: (Wife) Doctor, please save him! He drank the insecticide we keep for the paddy.

states.label: Partly atropinised
states.appearance: Still wet and noisy, a little more alert.

exam.PULM: Fewer crackles, but still present in both lungs.

exam.GENERAL: More alert. Mouth dry. No drooling.
exam.PULM: Chest clear. No crackles or wheeze.
exam.SKIN: Axillae dry. A few fasciculations remain.

exam.NEURO: GCS 14. Neck flexion 4/5. Watch for intermediate syndrome.

exam.PULM: Crackles have come back in both lungs.

states.label: Atropine toxicity
states.appearance: Agitated and confused, picking at the sheets, hot and flushed.

exam.GENERAL: Agitated, confused, picking at the bedsheet.
exam.HEENT: Pupils dilated (6 mm). Mouth very dry.
exam.ABD: Distended. No bowel sounds. Bladder palpable.

states.patientSays: (Patient, shouting) Let me go! Who are you?

states.label: Respiratory failure
states.appearance: Unresponsive to voice, pooling secretions, barely breathing.

exam.GENERAL: Unresponsive to voice. Secretions pooling in the mouth.
exam.PULM: Very poor air entry. Copious secretions. Shallow breaths.
exam.NEURO: GCS 8. Weak cough. Cannot lift his head.

states.label: Intubated, still cholinergic
states.appearance: Intubated and ventilated. Copious secretions in the tube.

exam.PULM: Copious tracheal secretions. Crackles in both lungs.

states.label: Admitted to ICU/HDU
states.appearance: Stable on the trolley to ICU.
states.outcome: Atropinised and stable on an infusion; admitted to ICU/HDU with an intermediate-syndrome watch.

states.label: Transferred to ICU, ventilated
states.appearance: Ventilated, atropinised, on the way to ICU.
states.outcome: Intubated, atropinised and on an infusion; transferred to ICU for ventilation.

states.label: Death
states.outcome: Died from respiratory failure due to untreated cholinergic crisis.

history.answer: He drank from the insecticide bottle we keep for the paddy field. My brother is bringing the bottle.
About an hour ago, around 9 at night.
Half the bottle was empty. Maybe 100 mL.

samplePrompts: Did he take any tablets or alcohol?
history.answer: He had a little arrack in the evening. We did not find any tablets.
He vomited twice in the autorickshaw. It smelled strongly of the chemical.
No illness. He does not take any medicines.
He has been very worried about the crop loan for weeks. Tonight he said he could not go on.
No allergies that we know of.

resultsByState.*: Brother arrives with the bottle: quinalphos 25% EC, an organophosphate insecticide.
Sinus bradycardia 48. QTc 510 ms. No ST changes.
pH 7.31, pCO₂ 48 mmHg, pO₂ 62 mmHg (room air), HCO₃ 23, lactate 2.4.
resultsByState.resp_failure: pH 7.18, pCO₂ 72 mmHg, pO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃ 25, lactate 3.8. Acute respiratory acidosis with hypoxia.
resultsByState.atropinised: pH 7.38, pCO₂ 40 mmHg, pO₂ 92 mmHg (on oxygen), lactate 1.6.
resultsByState.maintained: pH 7.39, pCO₂ 39 mmHg, pO₂ 95 mmHg (on oxygen), lactate 1.4.
resultsByState.ventilated_atropinised: pH 7.36, pCO₂ 42 mmHg, pO₂ 110 mmHg (FiO₂ 0.4), lactate 1.8.

resultsByState.*: 410 U/L (reference 4,000–12,000). Confirms exposure. It does not guide atropine dosing.
WBC 13,800/µL, Hb 14.2 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, Na 138, K 3.6 mmol/L, amylase 260 U/L (raised, common in OP poisoning).
Bilateral perihilar haziness from secretions. No focal consolidation.
resultsByState.ventilated_crisis: Endotracheal tube 4 cm above the carina. Bilateral perihilar haziness.
resultsByState.ventilated_atropinised: Endotracheal tube 4 cm above the carina. Lungs clearer.

interventions.name: Decontaminate with staff PPE
interventions.dose: Gloves and gown for staff; remove soiled clothes; wash skin and hair with soap and water

feedbackByState.*: Clothes bagged and removed. Skin washed. Staff protected.
Secretions cleared for now. They will keep coming until he is atropinised.

interventions.name: Oxygen
interventions.dose: High flow, then titrate to SpO₂ 94–98%
interventions.notIndicatedReason: SpO₂ is already 96% or above. Oxygen is not needed right now.

feedbackByState.*: Two 18G cannulae in place: one for fluids, one for atropine. Monitor on.

interventions.name: Atropine bolus
interventions.dose: Start 1.8–3 mg; double the dose every 5 min until atropinised
interventions.contraindicationReason: He was already atropinised. More atropine bolus causes atropine toxicity: tachycardia, hyperthermia, delirium, ileus and urinary retention.

feedbackByState.cholinergic_crisis: Partial response: HR 72 but the chest is still wet. Reassess in 5 minutes and double the dose if not atropinised.
feedbackByState.partial_atropinisation: Doubled dose given. Chest clear, HR above 80, SBP above 80, axillae dry: atropinised.
feedbackByState.recurrent_crisis: Re-bolused until atropinised again. Increase the infusion rate by 20%.
feedbackByState.ventilated_crisis: Doubling doses given until the chest cleared and HR was above 80: atropinised.

interventions.name: Atropine infusion
interventions.dose: 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour
interventions.requiresMessage: Atropinise him with bolus doses first. The infusion only maintains atropinisation.
interventions.notIndicatedReason: Not atropinised yet. An infusion alone is too slow: keep giving doubling boluses first.

feedbackByState.atropinised: Infusion started at about 2 mg/hour (15% of the loading dose). Check chest, HR, pupils, axillae and bowel sounds every 15 minutes.
feedbackByState.ventilated_atropinised: Infusion started at about 2 mg/hour. Check for recurrence and toxicity every 15 minutes.

interventions.name: Stop atropine infusion for 30 minutes
interventions.dose: Then restart at a 20% lower rate
interventions.notIndicatedReason: There are no signs of atropine toxicity. Stopping now risks the cholinergic signs coming back.

interventions.name: Pralidoxime
interventions.dose: 30 mg/kg (1.8 g) over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h (about 480 mg/h)

feedbackByState.*: Given per local protocol. Evidence of benefit is uncertain; atropine and the airway come first.

interventions.name: Intubate: ketamine + rocuronium
interventions.dose: Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg, rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg; suction ready
interventions.notIndicatedReason: He is atropinised, protecting his airway and oxygenating. Intubation is not needed now.

feedbackByState.*: Tube passed. Copious secretions suctioned. Ventilator connected.

interventions.name: Intubate: ketamine + succinylcholine
interventions.contraindicationReason: Succinylcholine is broken down by plasma cholinesterase, which OP poisoning blocks. Paralysis can last for hours. Use rocuronium.

feedbackByState.*: Tube passed. Copious secretions suctioned. Ventilator connected.

interventions.name: Gastric lavage
interventions.contraindicationReason: Gastric lavage is not routinely recommended: no proven benefit, and a high risk of aspiration in a drowsy patient with heavy secretions.

interventions.name: Activated charcoal
interventions.notIndicatedReason: Charcoal has shown no clear benefit in OP poisoning, and it risks aspiration. Never give it before the airway is safe.

feedbackByState.*: ICU accepts. Ask for hourly atropine checks and a watch for intermediate syndrome (neck and proximal weakness, 24–96 hours).
MLC registered and police intimation sent as required.
Psychiatry referral planned for when he is medically fit. Wife counselled and supported.

transitions.message: Partial response to atropine. Keep doubling.
Atropinised: chest clear, HR above 80, SBP above 80.
Too much atropine: he is agitated, hot and tachycardic.
Infusion held. Toxicity settling; restart 20% lower in 30 minutes.
Without an infusion, the cholinergic signs are coming back.
Intubated and ventilated. Still needs atropine.
Intubated and ventilated. Still needs atropine.
Without an infusion, the secretions are returning.
He is barely breathing: respiratory failure.
Atropine was not escalated. He is barely breathing: respiratory failure.
Untreated cholinergic crisis on the ventilator: bradycardic arrest.

criticalActions.label: First atropine bolus within 5 minutes
criticalActions.teaching: Pinpoint pupils, secretions and bradycardia after a pesticide are enough to start atropine. Do not wait for the container or tests.

criticalActions.label: Atropine infusion after atropinisation
criticalActions.teaching: Once atropinised, run an infusion at 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour, or the signs come back.

criticalActions.label: Decontamination with staff protection
criticalActions.teaching: Remove soiled clothes and wash the skin, with gloves and a gown for staff. Do not delay atropine for this.

criticalActions.label: Oxygen for hypoxia
criticalActions.teaching: Give oxygen early, but atropine is what clears the bronchorrhoea.

criticalActions.label: IV fluid bolus
criticalActions.teaching: Give 10–20 mL/kg of saline early; many patients are dehydrated from vomiting, diarrhoea and sweating.

criticalActions.label: Succinylcholine avoided
criticalActions.teaching: OP poisoning blocks plasma cholinesterase, so succinylcholine causes prolonged paralysis. Use rocuronium.

criticalActions.label: Routine gastric lavage avoided
criticalActions.teaching: Lavage has no proven benefit and risks aspiration. Focus on atropine, oxygen and the airway.

criticalActions.label: Poison and timing identified
criticalActions.teaching: Ask what was taken, how much and when, and ask for the container. Treat the toxidrome meanwhile.

criticalActions.label: ICU/HDU admission
criticalActions.teaching: Admit to a monitored bed: recurrence, atropine toxicity and intermediate syndrome can all appear later.

criticalActions.label: Medico-legal case registered
criticalActions.teaching: In India, poisoning is a medico-legal case: register an MLC and inform the police as required.

criticalActions.label: Psychiatric assessment planned
criticalActions.teaching: Every intentional self-poisoning needs a psychiatric assessment and safety plan once medically fit.

criticalActions.label: Airway secured with rocuronium in respiratory failure
criticalActions.teaching: Intubate early for respiratory failure, low GCS or uncontrolled secretions. Use a non-depolarising agent.

criticalActions.label: Infusion held for atropine toxicity
criticalActions.teaching: For atropine toxicity (tachycardia, hyperthermia, delirium, no bowel sounds), stop the infusion for 30 minutes and restart 20% lower.

debrief.diagnosis: Acute organophosphate (quinalphos) self-poisoning with cholinergic crisis
debrief.summary: A 34-year-old farmer drank about 100 mL of quinalphos an hour before arrival. Pinpoint pupils, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, sweating and fasciculations make the cholinergic toxidrome clear. Survival depends on fast atropine titration, an infusion, and timely airway support.
debrief.disposition: Admit to ICU/HDU on an atropine infusion with checks every 15 minutes at first. Watch for intermediate syndrome for 24–96 hours (neck flexion and proximal weakness, cranial nerve palsies) and be ready to ventilate. Register an MLC. Arrange a psychiatric assessment once medically fit.
teachingPoints: Start atropine at 1.8–3 mg IV and double the dose every 5 minutes.
Targets: clear chest, HR above 80, SBP above 80, dry axillae, pupils no longer pinpoint. A clear chest matters most.
Once atropinised, infuse 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour.
If signs recur, re-bolus and raise the infusion by 20%. If toxicity appears, stop the infusion for 30 minutes and restart 20% lower.
Decontaminate with staff PPE. Do not perform routine gastric lavage.
Pralidoxime: evidence of benefit is uncertain; follow local protocol, but never delay atropine or the airway.
Cholinesterase levels confirm exposure but do not guide atropine dosing.
